PRO: We strongly affirm the resolution: European members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization should ratify the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.

To define our terms: to ratify means to formally consent to be bound by a treaty; European members of NATO are the 30 European allies in the 32-nation alliance; and the TPNW is the 2017 United Nations treaty outlawing the possession, hosting, or assistance of nuclear weapons. Nuclear deterrence is a gamble that demands a 100 percent success rate forever. We affirm for three reasons.

First, humanitarian risk and near misses. Deterrence has survived on luck, not genius. Lewis, 14 at Chatham House reviewed declassified evidence from 13 near-nuclear-use crises and found the world 'has, indeed, been lucky,' saved by individual officers acting 'often in disobedience of protocol and political guidance,' as in the 1983 Petrov false alarm. Today, Kristensen, 26 at the Federation of American Scientists estimates the US still stores about 100 B61 gravity bombs at six airbases in five European NATO countries, painting a first-strike bullseye on them. If that luck runs out once, the Red Cross (ICRC, 20) warns fallout 'cannot be contained within national borders,' and Nature Food modeling (Xia, Robock, and Toon, 22) estimates a US-Russia war could starve over 5 billion people. And those bombs buy nothing: Sweeney, 20 at Defense Priorities shows the jets carrying them cannot reliably get through Russian air defenses, and RAND's Baltic wargames found even modernized NATO tactical nukes leave Russia with escalation dominance (Davis, 19) — Russia can always raise the stakes one more level, so NATO is the side that backs down. Europe carries all the risk of being a target and none of the protection.

Second, Europe can stop an invasion without nuclear weapons. Here is what that means in a fight. To take ground, Russia has to push tanks, fuel, and ammunition forward in a constant stream down a handful of roads and rail lines. Cut that stream and the attack stops moving, because a tank with no fuel is a steel box. SIPRI, 26 shows NATO outspends Russia 1.58 trillion dollars to 190 billion, an 8.3-to-1 advantage, and the 29 European members alone spend 559 billion, up 14 percent in 2025. That money buys the tools that cut the stream: as van Hooft, 25 at RAND Europe explains, NATO's stealth fighters, air-and-missile defenses, and long-range precision missiles could target Russian units attacking NATO territory, their reinforcements, and their logistics. The jets get through to shoot, the defenses knock down the missiles aimed at our bases, and the long-range missiles kill the supply convoys before they reach the front. Russia loses the invasion, and nobody has to threaten millions of civilians to do it. And we keep the alliance: Harvard Law's clinic (Harvard Law Clinic, 18) confirms allies can stay in NATO's Article 5 conventional defense as long as they give up the nuclear umbrella and opt out of nuclear planning, like France since 1966.

Third, divestment and cutting off Russian nuclear revenue. We do not need Russia to sign for this to work. Article 1(1)(e) legally bans assisting nuclear weapons 'in any way,' which the Nuclear Weapons Ban Monitor reads to cover financing, putting legal pressure on Europe's banks. PAX/ICAN, 23 profile 109 financial institutions already restricting nuclear weapons producers, many citing the TPNW, and institutions holding 3.9 trillion dollars named the treaty as a reason to exclude them (PAX/ICAN, 22). More importantly, Danylyuk, 26 at the Royal United Services Institute reveals European Union nations still paid about 781 million euros in 2025 for enriched uranium and nuclear fuel from Russia's state corporation Rosatom, whose weapons complex employed about 38 percent of its 250,000 workers as of 2016, per SIPRI data. Europe is helping fund the arsenal it says it fears. So: stop paying the people who build Russia's warheads, stop being a target for weapons we cannot even use, and keep the forces that actually stop an invasion. We proudly affirm.
CON: We strongly negate the resolution: European members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization should ratify the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.

To define our terms: to ratify means to formally approve a treaty so the country becomes legally bound by it under international law; European members of NATO are all 30 European allies in the 32-nation alliance, including nuclear-armed Britain and France; and the TPNW is the 2017 United Nations treaty outlawing the possession, hosting, or assistance of nuclear weapons. Disarming European democracies one-sidedly does not make nuclear-armed autocracies lay down their weapons. As the North Atlantic Council, 20 officially warned, a world where the states that challenge the international rules-based order have nuclear weapons, but NATO does not, is not a safer world. Stripping Europe's deterrent creates a power vacuum for three reasons.

First, the TPNW hands Russia a 100 percent European nuclear monopoly and invites nuclear blackmail. The Pro side tries to shrink this resolution to forward-deployed B61 bombs, yet it binds all 30 European NATO members, and under TPNW Articles 1 and 4 that legally forces Britain and France to destroy all 515 of their sovereign warheads, most on survivable continuous-at-sea submarines (van Hooft, 25 at RAND), and strips every ratifying ally of the US nuclear umbrella, as even Harvard Law's pro-ban clinic concludes (Harvard Law Clinic, 18). That is especially dangerous when President Trump said of NATO allies, 'If they don't pay, I'm not going to defend them' (AP, 25), and former CIA Director Leon Panetta warned that 'a very nervous Europe believes that The United States would not stand behind Article Five' (Panetta, 25). Europe cannot afford to destroy Britain and France's independent submarine shield while Russia retains about 4,400 warheads, including roughly 1,800 tactical warheads (Kristensen, 26 at FAS). Against a monopoly, massed conventional brigades are wiped out by a single tactical strike, and Putin can issue one ultimatum threatening Warsaw or Vilnius to force Europe to capitulate without a shot — just as Ukraine was invaded after agreeing in 1994 to give up the Soviet nukes on its soil.

Second, nuclear deterrence prevents great-power war and stops proliferation. Before deterrence raised the cost of war, conventional wars in Europe killed tens of millions of people. The certainty of retaliation from American, British, and French forces is why zero inches of NATO territory covered by Article 5 have been invaded in 77 years. Jones, 25 at CSIS found Russian sabotage across Europe nearly tripled from 2023 to 2024, and testified in November 2025 that European militaries still lack enough air defense and long-range strike munitions. Stripping the nuclear shield lowers the threshold for invasion and triggers proliferation: as US support wavered in March 2025, Poland's prime minister told parliament Poland must reach for the most modern capabilities related to nuclear weapons (Tusk, 25).

Third, the TPNW only disarms accountable democracies while state-funded dictatorships ignore it. On divestment, Muñoz, 26 in the Don't Bank on the Bomb report admits the number of financial institutions backing nuclear weapons producers actually rose about 15 percent, from 260 to 301, and its list of 25 producers is dominated by Western contractors like BAE Systems, Leonardo, and Lockheed Martin that build NATO's conventional fighter jets and air defenses, with zero Russian companies on the list. Meanwhile, the SIPRI Yearbook, 26 confirms Russia, China, and North Korea keep modernizing their arsenals, with China and North Korea expanding them, through state-run complexes funded by state budgets, while the EU can sanction Rosatom's uranium trade directly (Danylyuk, 26 at RUSI) without ratifying a treaty that, as Hill, 21 at Chatham House confirms, failed to require compulsory IAEA Additional Protocol inspections globally. We proudly negate.
